Learning Objectives
Recognize pertinent patient history and physical examination findings that may be concerning
for osseous defects of the glenohumeral joint.
Differentiate the role of various imaging modalities in the diagnosis of bone loss and instability
of the glenohumeral joint.
Review methods to quantify bone loss via imaging studies and diagnostic arthroscopy.


Patient History
A thorough patient history and physical examination should be completed for all
patients. In the patient history, the mechanism of injury, the number of dislocations, and
the causes of apprehension should be determined. In patients with bone loss and
subsequent glenohumeral instability, provocative tests also may be helpful in
determining the diagnosis.
Physical Examination
The physical examination should include maneuvers to elicit additional information about the
injury and associated pathology. In addition to performing provocative tests on the affected
shoulder, a thorough examination should include evaluation of the neck and the contralateral
shoulder. The anterior apprehension, load-and-shift, and the anterior-posterior drawer tests
are the most common tests used to evaluate for shoulder instability.
Apprehension is much more likely to be diagnostic of shoulder instability than pain during
these provocative tests. The anterior apprehension test is performed by bringing the patient’s
shoulder into a position of 90° of abduction and 90° of external rotation. The test is positive if
the patient experiences a feeling of impending dislocation. Patients with substantial bone loss
often will have apprehension, similar to that noted in the anterior apprehension test, at
midrange of
The anterior apprehension, load-and-shift, and the anterior-posterior drawer tests are the
most common tests used to evaluate for shoulder instability. Apprehension is much more
likely to be diagnostic of shoulder instability than pain during these provocative tests. The
anterior apprehension test is performed by bringing the patient’s shoulder into a position of
90° of abduction and 90° of external rotation. The test is positive if the patient experiences a
feeling of impending dislocation. Patients with substantial bone loss often will have
apprehension, similar to that noted in the anterior apprehension test, at midrange of
abduction (ie, 45°).
The relocation test also can be used to evaluate for shoulder instability and bone loss. After a
positive examination is elicited, the position of 90-90 is maintained, and a posteriorly directed
force is applied. Resolution of guarding and apprehension is considered a positive test.

In patients with shoulder instability, evaluating for a sulcus sign also is important. The shoulder
is stabilized, and an inferior force is directed on the elbow. The test is positive if a dimple or
sulcus appears beneath the acromion as the humeral head is translated inferiorly
Evaluation and Diagnosis
Patterns of Bone Loss
Understanding the extent of glenoid bone loss is extremely important in the setting of
shoulder arthroplasty.
Glenoid bone loss may be a substantial contributor to shoulder instability.

Patterns of Bone Loss
In patients with an acute shoulder dislocation (<3 months), a bony Bankart lesion likely
will be observed on plain radiographs and CT scans; however, with time, the bony
fragment can resorb, and more erosive bone loss likely will be observed. Therefore, the
type of bone loss encountered in patients with shoulder instability can be attributed to
two separate mechanisms: acute setting with fracture fragments (bony Bankart) or
chronic setting with attritional glenoid bone loss. Well-established patterns also exist for
outlining glenoid bone loss.
Progressive bone loss secondary to primary glenohumeral arthritis is a common
progression of the disease. The Walch classification system is one of the most used
classification systems to outline glenoid bone loss in patients with glenohumeral arthritis
and is based on the location of wear. This classification system was modified to include
other types of wear. Patients with a type A glenoid have concentric wear, and the most
common site of wear is central on the glenoid. Type A is further subdivided into type A1
and type A2, with the difference being the amount of central bone loss that occurs. If
central wear is substantial enough that the anterior and posterior borders transect the
humeral head, the glenoid is classified as type A2. Patients with a type B glenoid have
more substantial posterior wear and subluxation. Patients with a type C glenoid have a
dysplastic glenoid. Patients with a type D glenoid have anterior subluxation1 (Figure 1;
Table 1).

Rotator cuff arthropathy may result in glenoid bone loss. In planning arthroplasty for the
management of rotator cuff arthropathy, surgeons must understand the extent of bone
loss. Although implants often have the option for augmentation during arthroplasty,
knowledge of where and when to use the augments preoperatively may be extremely
useful. The Sirveaux classification system is one of the more common classification
systems used to evaluate glenoid bone loss in patients with rotator cuff arthropathy. The
Sirveaux classification system is based on the E scale, with E standing for erosion. Type
E0 is used if no glenoid erosion is observed. Type E1 describes concentric erosion. Type
E2 describes superior erosion. Type E3 describes superior erosion that extends to the
inferior rim. Finally, type E4 describes erosion isolated to the inferior part of the glenoid.
Inflammatory arthritis also may cause glenoid bone loss, with rheumatoid arthritis being
the most common inflammatory condition leading to shoulder arthroplasty.
Revision arthroplasty may lead to bone loss and often may be considerable. Focus
should be on removing the existing implant while attempting to preserve as much native
bone as possible. In addition, attempting to evaluate the bone stock with the index
components in place may be difficult because projection from the metal components
may interfere with CT scans. Wagner et al2 developed an algorithm to determine the
extent of bone loss, specifically during revision to reverse total shoulder arthroplasty.
Classification only takes place after the previous implant has been removed along with
all cement and initial reaming has been completed. Bone loss is based on location and

Imaging Modalities
Radiography

Radiography
Plain radiography is an inexpensive method for detecting humeral and glenoid bone
loss. A true AP view (Grashey view) can detect Hill-Sachs lesions. An AP radiograph can
detect bony Bankart lesions. An axillary lateral view affords visualization of the humeral

a West Point view, and Bernageau view allow for assessment of anterior glenoid rim

Computed Tomography

Computed Tomography
CT is the preferred imaging modality to assess for glenoid bone loss and humeral head
bone loss, and contralateral CT scans of the glenohumeral joint may aid in quantifying
the amount of glenoid bone loss in the involved shoulder. An en-face sagittal view with
three-dimensional reconstruction images and humeral head subtraction also can be
used to visualize the entire glenoid surface and assess for pathology, including bony
Bankart lesions, glenoid dysplasia, and glenoid bone loss.

Two frequently used methods to quantify bone loss include the PICO method and the
percentage of glenoid width loss.3 In the PICO method, a best-fit circle can be applied to
the inferior two-thirds of the glenoid. The amount of bone missing from the circle, as a
percentage of the total surface area of the inferior circle, is determined via digital
measurements. In the glenoid width loss method, the Griffith Index compares maximum
glenoid width side to side as a reference for bone loss. The Griffith Index considers the
differences in side-to-side height in the width ratio. Three-dimensional reconstruction
images are useful for quantifying the size of humeral head bone defects. The depth and
length of Hill-Sachs lesions and the percentage of involvement of the humeral head can
be quantified on axial and coronal CT scans.4 Saito et al5 described a method for
assessing humeral bone loss using a best-fit circle referenced off a clock starting from
the bicipital groove, which may be reproducible in the sagittal and axial planes.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is useful in the evaluation of soft-tissue structures of the shoulder joint. Magnetic
resonance arthrography often is the preferred imaging modality to assess for Bankart
lesions and other labral pathology.
Techniques

Techniques
Numerous methods have been developed to describe bone loss in patients with
recurrent shoulder instability. Burkhart and De Beer6 reported that a defect greater than
25% of glenoid width requires bone grafting. Rowe et al7 classified Hill-Sachs lesions into
three sizes: mild (2 cm × 0.3 cm), moderately severe (4 cm × 0.5 cm), and severe (4 cm × 1
cm or greater). With Bankart repair alone, the recurrence rate was zero in shoulders with
a mild Hill-Sachs lesion, whereas it was 4.7% and 6.0% in shoulders with moderately

severe and severe Hill-Sachs lesions, respectively. The authors concluded that a severe
Hill-Sachs lesion was a risk factor for recurrent shoulder instability after Bankart repair
and that an additional procedure to limit the humeral head defect from engaging should
be considered. The Hill Sachs interval is defined as the sum of the width of the Hill-Sachs
lesion and the bone bridge between the lateral esdge of the Hill -Sachs lesion and the
rotator cuff attachments.
The glenoid track theory was developed as an alternative option to describe the contact
area between the glenoid and the humeral head as it relates to instability. The glenoid
track constitutes 83% of glenoid width. This is because the glenoid pushes the cuff
posteriorly, and 17% of the glenoid width is lost. If bone loss occurs in the glenoid, then
the amount of bone loss is further subtracted by the remaining 83% that constitutes the
glenoid track. As the arm is elevated, the glenoid shifts from the inferomedial to the
superolateral portion of the posterior articular surface of the humeral head. Lesions on
the humeral head are separated into two groups: off-track and on-track lesions. The
track itself is the humeral head articular surface; if a Hill-Sachs lesion is present,
surgeons can assess the risk of the lesion engaging with the glenoid based on the track.
If a Hills-Sachs lesion is on-track (ie, lies within the portion of the humeral head articular
surface that articulates with the glenoid), then it will not engage. If a Hill-Sachs lesion is
off-track (ie, located closer to the edge of the glenoid), the likelihood of it engaging is
higher.7 Radiographs can be used to determine if a Hill-Sachs lesion is on track or off
track. If a Hill-Sachs lesion is less than the glenoid track, then the lesion is on-track. If a
Hill-Sachs lesion is greater than the glenoid track, then the lesion is considered to be off-
track (Video 2).

Proposed Treatment Algorithm
Zero to 10% glenoid bone loss and an on-track Hill-Sachs lesion indicates arthroscopic Bankart
repair.3,8,9
10% to 20% glenoid bone loss with good tissue quality, with or without an off-track Hill-Sachs
lesion, indicates arthroscopic Bankart repair with or without double-row stabilization or
remplissage.
Greater than 20% glenoid bone loss and an on-track Hill-Sachs lesion indicates open reduction
and internal fixation of bony Bankart lesion (if present) versus Latarjet procedure.
Greater than 20% glenoid bone loss and an off-track Hill-Sachs lesion indicates Latarjet
procedures with or without remplissage/humeral head allografting.
